title: Precision Dosing in Presence of Multiobjective Therapies by Integrating Reinforcement Learning and PK-PD Models: Application to Givinostat Treatment of Polycythemia Vera

content.abstract_summary: Applies Q-learning (QL) integrated with a population PK-PD model to the multiobjective adaptive dosing problem for givinostat (HDAC inhibitor) in polycythemia vera (PV). PV treatment must simultaneously normalize three hematological parameters (PLT, WBC, HCT) as both efficacy and toxicity endpoints. The MDP state space is 487 states; 7 dose levels (50–200 mg/day) are the actions. Two QL approaches: QL-agent (one agent trained on a population of 98 virtual patients) and QL-agents (one personal agent per patient). QL-agent achieves similar CHR to the clinical protocol (77% vs. 83%) with slightly worse safety. QL-agents outperform both: 93% CHR, 0% severe toxicities, median time to stable CHR 47 days vs. 99–105 days for comparators. Limitation: validated only in-silico; RUV excluded; individual PK-PD parameters assumed fully known.
key_findings: The givinostat adaptive dosing problem is formalized as an MDP with 487 states (PLT×WBC×HCT categories + previous dose + interruption flags), 7 dose-level actions, and a manually designed multi-term reward function balancing three simultaneous endpoints

Population-level QL-agent (trained on 98 virtual patients, evaluated on 10 test sets of 98 patients): 77% CHR vs. 83% for the clinical Phase III protocol — statistically similar efficacy but higher severe toxicity rate (40.30% vs. 14.28%)

The QL-agent notably learned the same dose-maintenance rule as the clinical protocol when parameters are in the efficacy range — a nontrivial validation of the RL framework's ability to rediscover clinical knowledge from scratch

Personal QL-agents (one per patient, trained on patient-specific PK-PD model simulations): 93% CHR vs. 79% (population QL-agent) vs. 75% (clinical protocol); median time to stable CHR 47 days vs. 99–105 days; 0% severe toxicities

Computational cost: training 98 personal QL-agents + 1 population agent simultaneously took 26 and 52 days respectively on an 8-core i7 Linux machine (3.6 GHz) using NONMEM 7.3.0 + MATLAB — a practical barrier to clinical translation
Key unresolved limitation: residual unexplained variability (RUV) was not simulated; adding RUV may require switching from tabular QL to stochastic RL variants or POMDP formulations

The study provides one of the first RL applications to a true multiobjective precision dosing problem with 3 simultaneous biomarkers — a more realistic oncology scenario than prior single-biomarker work
limitations: Residual unexplained variability (RUV) excluded from simulations — deterministic PK-PD assumed; RUV introduction may require switching from tabular QL to stochastic RL or POMDP
Individual PK-PD parameters assumed fully known from treatment start — in practice, Bayesian estimation would be needed to progressively update individual parameters
Not validated on real clinical data; all results are in-silico based on a published givinostat population PK-PD model
Computational time (26–52 days) is impractical for real-time clinical deployment; efficient implementation on high-performance computing is needed
State space (487 states) and reward function are manually designed and specific to givinostat clinical context — generalizability to other drugs/biomarkers not demonstrated

extracted_claims.text: "QL-agent learned a general adaptive dosing protocol that achieved a similar CHR rate (77% vs. 83%) when compared to the actual givinostat clinical protocol on 10 simulated populations."

"These QL-based patient-specific adaptive dosing rules outperformed both the clinical protocol and QL-agent by reaching the CHR in 93% of the test patients and completely avoided severe toxicities during the whole treatment period."

"The QL-agent estimated the same dosing rules of the clinical protocol for all patient efficacy status (i.e., maintaining the current dose level) — a confirmation of the powerfulness of RL algorithms that are able to learn from scratch a set of reasonable rules close to those formulated on the basis of the clinical knowledge."
"Defining a clinical trial setup that meets current regulatory standards to evaluate model-informed RL approaches for precision dosing remains one of the most important and challenging open issues."

gaps_addressed: Most complete current proof-of-concept of RL+PK-PD for precision dosing — the computational cost (26–52 days) quantifies the MCS WG's Pillar 3 target: efficient RL implementations using surrogate models or faster simulation engines

The manually designed 3-endpoint reward function and 487-state MDP are exactly where MCS's mathematical expertise (optimal control theory, MDP theory, Lyapunov-based reward design) can add rigor beyond current empirical approaches
